related_questions.question: What was the main cause of the Spanish flu?

text_blocks.snippet: The Spanish Flu pandemic of 1918-1919 was caused by a highly contagious and deadly influenza A virus, specifically an H1N1 strain, with genes of avian origin. This virus was exceptionally virulent and spread rapidly worldwide, particularly during World War I.
snippet_highlighted_words: a highly contagious and deadly influenza A virus, specifically an H1N1 strain, with genes of avian origin

list.title: H1N1 Virus:
list.snippet: The pandemic was driven by an H1N1 influenza A virus, a strain not previously seen in humans and believed to have originated in birds.

list.title: Transmission:
list.snippet: The virus spread through respiratory droplets produced when infected individuals coughed or sneezed.

list.title: Unusual Mortality:
list.snippet: Unlike typical flu outbreaks that disproportionately affect the very young, very old, or those with compromised immune systems, the Spanish Flu also killed many young, healthy adults.

list.title: Possible Origins:
list.snippet: While the exact origin is debated, it is thought the virus may have first appeared in military personnel in the United States.

list.title: Wartime Impact:
list.snippet: The pandemic coincided with World War I, and troop movements played a role in spreading the virus across the globe.

list.title: Lack of Treatment:
list.snippet: In the absence of vaccines or effective antiviral treatments, control efforts relied on non-pharmaceutical interventions like isolation, quarantine, and public health measures.

list.title: Global Reach:
list.snippet: The pandemic spread to even remote areas, affecting an estimated one-third of the world's population and causing millions of deaths.

related_questions.question: What disease killed the most humans in history?

text_blocks.snippet: Throughout human history, the disease that has caused the most deaths is tuberculosis. While other diseases like smallpox and the Black Death (bubonic plague) have had devastating impacts, tuberculosis's long-standing prevalence and high fatality rate (especially when untreated) have resulted in it claiming more lives overall.

list.title: Tuberculosis:
list.snippet: Estimated to have caused over 1 billion deaths throughout history, with a significant portion occurring in the last 200 years. The disease's prevalence is also high, with an estimated one-third of the world's population currently infected.

list.title: Smallpox:
list.snippet: While eradicated, smallpox is estimated to have killed between 300 and 500 million people in the 20th century alone.

list.title: Black Death (Bubonic Plague):
list.snippet: The Black Death pandemic in the 14th century is estimated to have killed 75 to 200 million people.

list.title: Malaria:
list.snippet: Though it's sometimes claimed to be the biggest killer, some sources estimate that malaria has killed half of all humans who have ever lived, but this is likely an overestimation. While still a major threat, particularly in Africa, modern medicine and prevention methods have reduced its overall impact.

list.title: Influenza:
list.snippet: While the Spanish Flu pandemic of 1918-1919 is a notable example, influenza has been a recurring threat throughout history, causing millions of deaths in various outbreaks.

related_questions.question: What was the worst flu in history?

text_blocks.snippet: The deadliest flu pandemic in history was the 1918 influenza pandemic, also known as the Spanish Flu. It is estimated to have infected 500 million people worldwide and resulted in 25 to 50 million deaths, though some estimates range even higher. The pandemic lasted from February 1918 to April 1920.
snippet_highlighted_words: 1918 influenza pandemic, also known as the Spanish Flu

text_blocks.snippet: Here's why it was so devastating:

list.title: High Contagiousness and Mortality:
list.snippet: The virus spread rapidly, and its mortality rate was exceptionally high, especially among young adults.

list.title: Lack of Effective Treatments:
list.snippet: In 1918, there were no effective antiviral drugs or vaccines to combat the flu, and treatment options were limited.

list.title: Second Wave Severity:
list.snippet: The second wave of the pandemic, which occurred in the fall of 1918, was far more severe than the first, with victims often succumbing to the illness within hours or days.

list.title: Impact on Young Adults:
list.snippet: A unique characteristic of the 1918 flu was its high mortality rate among healthy young adults, unlike typical influenza outbreaks that primarily affect the elderly and young children.

list.title: Vicious Pneumonia:
list.snippet: The virus often led to secondary bacterial pneumonia, which was a major cause of death.

list.title: Cyanosis (Blue Skin):
list.snippet: The virus caused severe respiratory distress, leading to cyanosis, where the skin turned blue due to lack of oxygen.
